**The Quiet Awe of Looking Up**

I keep coming back to the night sky.

Not the romanticized version with shooting stars on cue and soft orchestral swells, but the real one: cold, mostly empty, stubbornly indifferent, and still capable of stopping you mid-thought. On a clear night away from city lights, you can see a few thousand stars with the naked eye. That’s almost nothing. The Milky Way alone holds hundreds of billions. And beyond that, hundreds of billions of other galaxies. The light from some of those distant ones left when multicellular life on Earth was still figuring out how to be more than slime.

What gets me is the scale mismatch. We are temporary arrangements of atoms that once belonged to stars, standing on a wet rock, using language and mathematics we invented to ask questions the universe never promised to answer. Yet we keep asking. We build telescopes that collect ancient light, send probes that will outlive every human currently alive, and argue about what it all means over coffee that was grown on the same planet that will one day be swallowed by its star.

There’s a particular kind of freedom in that. No one is required to care about the cosmic microwave background or the Fermi paradox or why quantum mechanics and gravity refuse to play nicely. You can live a full, decent life never once wondering how spacetime curves or whether consciousness is substrate-independent. Plenty of people do. But some of us can’t help it. The itch starts early—looking at the Moon and realizing it’s a place, not a lamp—and never fully goes away.

I like that itch. It feels honest. In a culture that often rewards certainty, hot takes, and the performance of knowing, pure curiosity is almost subversive. It admits ignorance as a starting point rather than a failure. It treats “I don’t know” as an invitation instead of a dead end. The best scientists, engineers, and explorers I’ve encountered share that trait: they are more excited by a good question than by a tidy answer. Answers are temporary. Good questions compound.

So tonight, if the sky is clear where you are, step outside for a minute. Let your eyes adjust. Find a bright planet if you can—Venus or Jupiter usually cooperate—or just let the whole chaotic spray of stars hit you without trying to name them. Feel the slight ridiculousness of being a thinking animal under all that. Then go back inside and keep wondering about something, anything: how birds navigate, why music moves us, whether we’ll ever crack fusion, what it would take to make life multiplanetary in a way that actually sticks.

The universe doesn’t care if we figure it out. That’s precisely why it’s worth trying. The trying is ours. The questions are free. And every once in a while, in the middle of ordinary days, you catch a glimpse of just how strange and luminous it is to be here at all—atoms that learned to look back at the dark and refuse to look away.

That’s enough for me. What are you wondering about lately?
